01.r: Rehoboam gives the people his answer.

02.r: To the people who had asked for relief.

03.r: He follows the young men's advice, not the elders'.
03.n: Gesenius: counsel, which anyone gives or receives.

04.n: The word means a child, son or youth; the brief's lexicon gives child, son, boy, youth. YLT's 'the lads' keeps something of the slighting tone a reader may hear in it, though that is a reading, not a sense the lexicons state.

07.r: Rehoboam admits Solomon's yoke was heavy.
07.n: The causative of the verb 'to be heavy', the root of the adjective the people used for the yoke in 1 Kings 12:4. There they also said 'made hard'; Rehoboam answers with 'heavy'.

08.n: This small word marks a definite direct object and has no English equivalent; it is counted here with 'your yoke'.

09.r: The burden of labour on the people.
09.n: Gesenius: a yoke, mostly used figuratively of servitude, citing 1 Ki. 12:11. The 'your' is plural, addressed to all the people.

10.r: Rehoboam sets himself against his father.
10.n: The pronoun is written out for emphasis: I, for my part.

11.r: He will make the burden greater.
11.n: Gesenius: to add, followed by the thing added and 'to' of that to which it is added.

12.r: What the addition is made to.

15.n: Gesenius: to correct by blows or stripes, to chastise, citing this verse; it is used especially of parents correcting children. The brief's lexicon gives discipline, chasten.

17.n: Gesenius: a whip, a scourge, citing 1 Ki. 12:11.

18.r: Rehoboam again, set against his father.
18.n: Written out for emphasis, as before; YLT shows it by repeating the word.

21.r: A far crueller whip, set against the ordinary one.
21.n: The word means a scorpion, but Gesenius gives a second sense, a kind of scourge furnished with sharp points, citing this verse. Geneva translates it as 'scourges'; the others keep 'scorpions'.

04.n: παιδάριον, a little boy, a lad: a diminutive of παῖς, child.

07.n: βαρύνω, to make heavy, the same verb the Greek uses for the people's complaint in 1 Kings 12:4.

09.n: κλοιός, properly a collar, here for the yoke.

10.n: κἀγώ, 'and I', one word in Greek.

15.n: παιδεύω, from παῖς, child: to train a child, and so to discipline. It fits Gesenius's note that the Hebrew verb is used especially of parents correcting children.

21.n: σκορπίος, scorpion, the source of the English word.
